---
title: "Weights and robust standard errors"
description: >
  How anova_bin(), anova_count() and anova_glm() read prior weights as
  frequencies, trials or sampling weights, what happens to zero weights, and
  where vcov_type's robust covariance reaches and when it is not used.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

```{r libs}
library(anovakit)
```

Three functions take prior weights and four take a robust covariance.

## Which functions take weights

| Function | `weights` | `vcov_type` |
|---|---|---|
| `anova_bin()` | yes | yes |
| `anova_count()` | yes | yes |
| `anova_glm()` | yes | yes |
| `anova_ancova()` | no | yes |

`weights` names a numeric column of the data, not a vector. The weights are
then subsetted with the rows, so they stay aligned when a row is dropped for a
missing value; a vector evaluated against the original data would not. The
column must be numeric and non-negative, and it cannot also be the response, a
grouping column or the offset. A missing or infinite weight is treated like a
missing value in any other analysed column: the row is dropped and counted in
`$n_removed`.

## How the weights are read

What a weight means depends on the weights and on the response. The package
decides which reading applies and says so in `$notes` when the reading
changes a result: the Pearson dispersion in `anova_count()`, the robust
covariance, and weights that are not whole numbers.

| The weights are | On | Read as | Each row is |
|---|---|---|---|
| whole numbers, some above 1 | a 0/1 response (binomial, quasi-binomial) or counts (Poisson, quasi-Poisson, negative binomial) | frequency weights | that many identical observations |
| whole numbers | a proportion (binomial) | numbers of trials | one binomial observation |
| not all whole numbers, or any weights in another family | any response | weights used as given, as `glm()` uses them | one unit |

`anova_bin()` always has a 0/1 response and `anova_count()` always has
counts, so in those two functions whole-number weights are always
frequencies. `anova_glm()` also takes proportions, where whole-number
weights are trials, and the Gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gaussian and `quasi()`
families, where they are precision weights. In both cases each row stays one
unit.

## Frequency weights

A frequency weight says how many identical observations a row stands for.
`UCBAdmissions` is a table of 4,526 applications to graduate school at
Berkeley in 1973, by gender, department and outcome. As a data frame it has
one row per cell and the count in `Freq`:

```{r ucb}
ucb <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions)
head(ucb)
c(rows = nrow(ucb), applicants = sum(ucb$Freq))
```

For comparison, here is the same data with one row per applicant:

```{r applicants}
applicants <- ucb[rep(seq_len(nrow(ucb)), ucb$Freq),
                  c("Admit", "Gender", "Dept")]
row.names(applicants) <- NULL
nrow(applicants)
```

The 24-row table with `weights = "Freq"` and the 4,526 rows without weights
give the same analysis:

```{r ucb-fits}
from_table <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                        success = "Admitted", plots = FALSE)
from_rows <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"),
                       success = "Admitted", plots = FALSE)
all.equal(from_table$anova, from_rows$anova)
data.frame(comparison = from_table$effect_sizes$comparison,
           or_table = from_table$effect_sizes$odds_ratio,
           or_rows = from_rows$effect_sizes$odds_ratio,
           se_table = from_table$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           se_rows = from_rows$effect_sizes$se_log_or)
c(table = from_table$model_stats$BIC, rows = from_rows$model_stats$BIC)
```

The odds ratios and standard errors agree to about six significant figures;
the rest is `glm()`'s convergence tolerance. BIC agrees too, because with
frequency weights its penalty uses the `r format(sum(ucb$Freq), big.mark = ",")`
observations the weights represent, not the `r nrow(ucb)` rows. The marginal
means, the comparisons and the observed proportions in
`$assumptions$proportions` match in the same way.

Counts work the same way in `anova_count()`. `InsectSprays` has 72 insect
counts, 12 for each of six sprays. Tabulated, it becomes one row per spray and
count, with the frequency in `Freq`:

```{r spray-table}
spray_tab <- as.data.frame(table(spray = InsectSprays$spray,
                                 count = InsectSprays$count),
                           stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
spray_tab$count <- as.numeric(spray_tab$count)
c(rows = nrow(spray_tab), nonzero_rows = sum(spray_tab$Freq > 0),
  observations = sum(spray_tab$Freq))
```

```{r spray-fits}
spray_rows <- anova_count(InsectSprays, "count", "spray", plots = FALSE)
spray_freq <- anova_count(spray_tab, "count", "spray", weights = "Freq",
                          plots = FALSE)
c(rows = spray_rows$model_type, table = spray_freq$model_type)
c(rows = spray_rows$dispersion, table = spray_freq$dispersion)
all.equal(spray_rows$anova, spray_freq$anova)
all.equal(spray_rows$effect_sizes, spray_freq$effect_sizes)
all.equal(spray_rows$emmeans, spray_freq$emmeans)
grep("frequency weights", spray_freq$notes, value = TRUE)
```

The Pearson dispersion, on which `model = "auto"` chooses between Poisson and
negative binomial, divides by the observations minus the parameters. Divided
by the rows of the table instead, it would be larger, and could switch the
model for no reason in the data. In `anova_glm()` the residual degrees of
freedom are counted in observations in the same way, so a quasi-Poisson or
quasi-binomial fit, an F test and a t interval on a frequency table equal
those of the expanded data. `$model` is still the `glm` that `stats::glm()`
fitted to the rows, and `$notes` says when its own `summary()` would
differ.

The [counts walkthrough](counts.html) shows the
`$assumptions$cell_counts` table and the `observed` plot for a frequency
table.

## Zero weights

`spray_tab` above still holds the combinations of spray and count that never
occurred, with a frequency of zero. A row with weight zero contributes nothing
to the fit, so it is dropped before fitting and counted in `$n_removed`:

```{r zero}
c(supplied = nrow(spray_tab), used = nrow(spray_freq$data_used),
  removed = spray_freq$n_removed)
grep("zero", spray_freq$notes, value = TRUE)
```

Keeping those rows would make the row counts, the robust standard errors and
the information criteria disagree with the fit. As for every function,
`nrow($data_used) + $n_removed` is the number of rows supplied.

A group whose weights are all zero is dropped from the analysis, and the note
names it:

```{r zero-group}
no_f <- spray_tab
no_f$Freq[no_f$spray == "F"] <- 0
grep("Level", anova_count(no_f, "count", "spray", weights = "Freq",
                          plots = FALSE)$notes, value = TRUE)
```

When every weight is zero, or only one row has a non-zero weight, the function
stops with an error.

## Trials behind proportions

A binomial response can be given as a proportion, with the number of trials
behind each proportion as the weight. That form is for `anova_glm()`:
`anova_bin()` takes a 0/1 response only. `esoph` is a case-control study of
oesophageal cancer, with the numbers of cases and controls in each of 88
combinations of age group, alcohol and tobacco consumption:

```{r esoph}
es <- esoph
es$agegp <- factor(es$agegp, ordered = FALSE)
es$alcgp <- factor(es$alcgp, ordered = FALSE)
es$trials <- es$ncases + es$ncontrols
es$prop <- es$ncases / es$trials
head(es[, c("agegp", "alcgp", "ncases", "trials", "prop")])
```

(The factors are made unordered so that the coefficients are comparisons with
the first level rather than polynomial trends.) With one row per subject
instead, the same data have `r sum(es$trials)` rows of a 0/1 response:

```{r esoph-long}
per_subject <- rbind(
  data.frame(agegp = rep(es$agegp, es$ncases),
             alcgp = rep(es$alcgp, es$ncases), case = 1),
  data.frame(agegp = rep(es$agegp, es$ncontrols),
             alcgp = rep(es$alcgp, es$ncontrols), case = 0))
nrow(per_subject)
```

```{r esoph-fits}
as_prop <- anova_glm(es, "prop", c("agegp", "alcgp"), family = binomial(),
                     weights = "trials", plots = FALSE)
as_rows <- anova_glm(per_subject, "case", c("agegp", "alcgp"),
                     family = binomial(), plots = FALSE)
all.equal(as_prop$anova, as_rows$anova)
data.frame(term = as_prop$emmeans$term,
           level = ifelse(is.na(as_prop$emmeans$agegp),
                          as.character(as_prop$emmeans$alcgp),
                          as.character(as_prop$emmeans$agegp)),
           prob_prop = as_prop$emmeans$estimate,
           prob_rows = as_rows$emmeans$estimate)
```

The likelihood-ratio tests and the marginal means are the same. The
deviance explained is not: it is measured against the saturated model, which
differs between the two forms, and a note says so. McFadden's R squared is
computed from the Bernoulli log-likelihood and is the same either way.

The trials are not frequencies, because each row is one binomial observation
rather than a count of identical ones. The Pearson dispersion of the
proportions carries information about overdispersion, which a 0/1 response
cannot show, so `anova_glm()` checks it:

```{r esoph-dispersion}
as_prop$assumptions$dispersion
grep("Pearson dispersion", as_prop$notes, value = TRUE)
```

A robust covariance also treats each of the `r nrow(es)` rows as one unit, so
it allows for the extra variation between rows that the dispersion of
`r round(as_prop$assumptions$dispersion, 2)` measures. The per-subject form
cannot see that variation, and its robust standard errors stay close to the
model-based ones:

```{r esoph-robust}
prop_hc3 <- anova_glm(es, "prop", c("agegp", "alcgp"), family = binomial(),
                      weights = "trials", vcov_type = "HC3", plots = FALSE)
rows_hc3 <- anova_glm(per_subject, "case", c("agegp", "alcgp"),
                      family = binomial(), vcov_type = "HC3", plots = FALSE)
data.frame(term = as_prop$emmeans$term,
           se_model = as_prop$emmeans$se,
           se_hc3_prop = prop_hc3$emmeans$se,
           se_hc3_rows = rows_hc3$emmeans$se)
```

Trials do not inflate the tests the way unequal sampling weights do (below):
they set the variance of each proportion, as precision weights do.

## Sampling and other weights that are not whole numbers

Weights that are not whole numbers are used as given, as `stats::glm()` uses
prior weights: each row's contribution to the likelihood is multiplied by its
weight, as if it were that many observations. The fit, the tests, the
intervals and the marginal means all treat them that way. The robust
covariance treats each row as one unit instead, and two checks rescale the
weights to average 1 first: the sparse-data check of `anova_bin()` and the
Pearson dispersion on which `anova_count()` chooses its model.

Suppose the applicants above came from a survey that sampled men at a higher
rate than women, so that each woman's response is weighted up and each man's
down. The weights here are made up for illustration and average 1:

```{r sampling-weights}
applicants$w <- c(Male = 0.4, Female = 2.2)[as.character(applicants$Gender)]
applicants$w <- applicants$w / mean(applicants$w)
tapply(applicants$w, applicants$Gender, unique)
```

### Their scale matters

Weights used as given have no natural scale, and the tests scale with them.
The same weights divided by 100 make the 4,526 applicants count as about 45,
and every likelihood-ratio statistic falls by the same factor:

```{r scale}
sw <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "w",
                success = "Admitted", plots = FALSE)
applicants$w_small <- applicants$w / 100
sw_small <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"),
                      weights = "w_small", success = "Admitted",
                      plots = FALSE)
data.frame(term = sw$anova$term, mean_1 = sw$anova$statistic,
           mean_0.01 = sw_small$anova$statistic)
grep("average", sw_small$notes, value = TRUE)
```

`anova_bin()`, `anova_count()` and a Poisson or binomial `anova_glm()` give
that note whenever such weights do not average 1 (within about 10%).
Rescale sampling weights to average 1, as above, or analyse them with a
design-based method such as `survey::svyglm()`.

In a binomial model, weights that are not whole numbers also make AIC, BIC
and the log-likelihood in `$model_stats` `NA`, with a note, because R's
binomial log-likelihood rounds the weights. McFadden's R squared and the
model-versus-null test use the deviances and are reported. `glm()`'s warning
about "non-integer #successes" is recorded in `$notes` rather than printed.

In `anova_count()` the Pearson dispersion in `$dispersion` and
`$model_dispersion` is computed with the weights rescaled to average 1, so the
choice between Poisson and negative binomial does not depend on their scale.
In `anova_glm()` the dispersion is that of the model as weighted, so in a
Poisson or binomial fit it scales with the weights, and so does the
overdispersion check; the note on the weights' scale says so. A family that
estimates its dispersion (Gaussian, Gamma, quasi families) absorbs the scale
of the weights.

### Unequal weights distort the tests

Weights that average 1 still distort the tests when they are unequal: some
terms are inflated, others deflated. A likelihood-ratio or Wald test treats
a woman's row, of weight `r sprintf("%.2f", max(applicants$w))`, as that many
independent observations, while it is one person. How much that moves a test
depends on where the heavy rows fall, so `$notes` computes the factor for
each term from the sandwich covariance:

```{r inflation}
sw$anova
grep("unequal", sw$notes, value = TRUE)
```

The calculation assumes the weights are not inverse variances; precision
weights, such as the trials behind a proportion, would not inflate the tests.
The note appears in `anova_bin()`, `anova_count()` and `anova_glm()` for
Poisson, quasi-Poisson, negative binomial, binomial and quasi-binomial fits
(on a binomial, only for weights that are not whole numbers on a 0/1
response). It never appears for Gaussian, Gamma or inverse Gaussian fits,
where weights are read as precision weights. It is given only when some test
would reject 7.5% or more of true null hypotheses at a nominal 5%. Under the
quasi families' F tests the estimated dispersion removes the average
inflation but not the part due to unequal weights, and the note says so.

The remedy the note names is a robust covariance, and an omnibus test that
uses it:

```{r inflation-fix}
sw_hc3 <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "w",
                    success = "Admitted", vcov_type = "HC3",
                    test_statistic = "Wald", plots = FALSE)
sw_hc3$anova
data.frame(comparison = sw$effect_sizes$comparison,
           se_model = sw$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           se_hc3 = sw_hc3$effect_sizes$se_log_or)
grep("unequal", sw_hc3$notes, value = TRUE)
```

Dept, the term the note names as the worst affected (its factor is the
larger one), falls from `r round(sw$anova$statistic[2])` to
`r round(sw_hc3$anova$statistic[2])`;
Gender rises from `r sprintf("%.2f", sw$anova$statistic[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", sw_hc3$anova$statistic[1])`. Those are the directions of
the note's factors, but the sizes differ from them, because the comparison
also moves from a likelihood-ratio to a Wald statistic. Most standard errors
grow, and the inflation note is gone.
Weights alone do not describe strata or clusters; a design-based analysis
with survey accounts for those too.

## Robust standard errors with `vcov_type`

`vcov_type = "model"` (the default) uses the model's own covariance.
`"HC0"` to `"HC4"` use a heteroscedasticity-consistent (sandwich) covariance
from the sandwich package, which does not rely on the family's variance
function or on equal residual variances. HC0 is White's estimator; HC1 to
HC4 refine it for small samples, HC1 by a degrees-of-freedom factor and HC2
to HC4 by each row's leverage. HC3, the default of `sandwich::vcovHC()` and
the type used throughout this guide, is the usual choice for small or
unbalanced groups.

The robust covariance does not reach every table:

| Result | `anova_ancova()` | `anova_bin()` | `anova_count()` | `anova_glm()` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Coefficients | no coefficient table | `$effect_sizes` (odds ratios) | `$effect_sizes` (rate ratios) | `$assumptions$coefficients` |
| `$emmeans` and `$posthoc` | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Omnibus `$anova` | yes, as Wald F tests | with `test_statistic = "Wald"` | with `test_statistic = "Wald"` | with `test_statistic = "Wald"` |
| `$simple_slopes` | yes | no such table | no such table | no such table |
| Not reached | `$effect_sizes`, `$slopes_test` | `$anova` unless `test_statistic = "Wald"` | `$anova` unless `test_statistic = "Wald"`; `$dispersion` and the model choice | `$anova` unless `test_statistic = "Wald"`; `$effect_sizes` |

In `anova_bin()`, `anova_count()` and `anova_glm()`, a likelihood-ratio or F
test compares deviances, so it rests on the model-based variance whatever
`vcov_type` says; set `test_statistic = "Wald"` for an omnibus test that uses
the robust covariance. `$notes` says which tests use it. Coefficient
intervals in `anova_bin()` and `anova_glm()` become Wald intervals built from
it, since a profile likelihood cannot use a sandwich covariance.

On `warpbreaks` (numbers of warp breaks per loom, 9 looms in each of six
cells), the default likelihood-ratio table is unchanged by `vcov_type`, while
a Wald table uses it:

```{r count-robust}
breaks_model <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                            interaction = TRUE, plots = FALSE)
breaks_lr <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                         interaction = TRUE, vcov_type = "HC3",
                         plots = FALSE)
breaks_wald <- anova_count(warpbreaks, "breaks", c("wool", "tension"),
                           interaction = TRUE, vcov_type = "HC3",
                           test_statistic = "Wald", plots = FALSE)
all.equal(breaks_model$anova, breaks_lr$anova)
breaks_wald$anova
data.frame(comparison = breaks_model$effect_sizes$comparison,
           low_model = breaks_model$effect_sizes$conf_low,
           high_model = breaks_model$effect_sizes$conf_high,
           low_hc3 = breaks_lr$effect_sizes$conf_low,
           high_hc3 = breaks_lr$effect_sizes$conf_high)
grep("omnibus", breaks_lr$notes, value = TRUE)
```

In `anova_ancova()` the omnibus table itself changes: its F tests become Wald
F tests built from the robust covariance (through `car::Anova(vcov. = )`), on
the model's residual degrees of freedom, so the table has no sums of squares.
Its `statistic` attribute, which `print()` shows in the heading, says so.
`MASS::anorexia` has the weights of 72 young women before and after one of
three treatments:

```{r ancova-robust}
an <- MASS::anorexia
an_hc3 <- anova_ancova(an, "Postwt", "Treat", "Prewt",
                       force_interaction = TRUE, vcov_type = "HC3",
                       plots = FALSE)
an_hc3$anova
attr(an_hc3$anova, "statistic")
grep("Wald F", an_hc3$notes, value = TRUE)
```

`$effect_sizes` are still computed from the model-based sums of squares,
which the covariance does not change, and the homogeneity-of-slopes test
stays the model-based F test. In `anova_ancova()` and in a Gaussian
`anova_glm()`, comparisons that use robust standard errors keep the model's
residual degrees of freedom, and a note warns that with very small groups of
unequal variance they can be anti-conservative; for a one-way design without
covariates, `anova_welch()` is better calibrated.

### Robust standard errors and weights

With frequency weights the sandwich is computed per observation, as it would
be on the data expanded to one row per observation. `sandwich::vcovHC()`
applied to the weighted rows directly would count each row as one unit with
an inflated score, and overstate the standard errors:

```{r freq-robust}
table_hc3 <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                       success = "Admitted", vcov_type = "HC3",
                       plots = FALSE)
appl_hc3 <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"),
                      success = "Admitted", vcov_type = "HC3",
                      plots = FALSE)
naive <- sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(from_table$model, type = "HC3")))[-1]
data.frame(comparison = table_hc3$effect_sizes$comparison,
           model_based = from_table$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           hc3_table = table_hc3$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           hc3_rows = appl_hc3$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           hc3_row_by_row = unname(naive))
grep("frequency weights represent", table_hc3$notes, value = TRUE)
```

The HC3 standard errors from the table and from one row per applicant are
the same. `sandwich::vcovHC()` on the table is wrong by a factor of
`r round(min(naive / table_hc3$effect_sizes$se_log_or))` to
`r round(max(naive / table_hc3$effect_sizes$se_log_or))`.

With any other weights (sampling weights, precision weights, trials) the
robust covariance treats each row as one independent unit, and `$notes`
says so. If such weights in fact count identical observations, expand the
data to one row per observation first.

## When the model-based covariance is used instead

In some fits a sandwich covariance is wrong, and the function uses the
model-based covariance instead, with a note saying why. That happens when:

- the sandwich package is not installed;
- some fitted values are on the boundary: a group with no events or all
  events in a binomial model, a group of all-zero counts, or a separated
  coefficient, where the sandwich collapses towards zero and gives
  spuriously small p-values;
- a row has leverage 1, as a group or cell with a single observation does,
  so its residual is zero by construction and the sandwich would give a
  standard error of zero (HC0, HC1) or none at all (HC2 to HC4);
- the robust covariance fails or has non-finite entries.

A site where nothing happened puts the fitted rate on the boundary:

```{r fallback-boundary}
incidents <- data.frame(
  site = rep(c("north", "south", "east"), each = 8),
  events = c(2, 4, 3, 1, 5, 3, 2, 4,
             6, 3, 5, 7, 4, 6, 5, 8,
             0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0))
grep("Robust", anova_count(incidents, "events", "site", vcov_type = "HC3",
                           plots = FALSE)$notes, value = TRUE)
```

A group with one observation has leverage 1:

```{r fallback-leverage}
small <- data.frame(g = c(rep("a", 6), rep("b", 6), "c"),
                    y = c(1:6, 3:8, 4))
grep("Robust", anova_glm(small, "y", "g", vcov_type = "HC3",
                         plots = FALSE)$notes, value = TRUE)
```

In `anova_ancova()`, `car::Anova()` refuses robust Wald tests for a model with
aliased coefficients (an empty cell of the design, for example). `$anova` then
keeps the model-based F tests, and `$notes` says so, while `$emmeans` and
`$posthoc` still use the robust covariance.
